Power vacuum.q: After the Mongol khanates collapsed, Turkic dynasties quickly seized Anatolia, Persia and northern India. Which idea best explains this?
Power vacuum.right: New states filled a power vacuum
wrong: Mongol khans gave the regions away
The Mongols did not hand over their lands; their empire fell apart and others took the space.
Europeans conquered the Mongol lands first
Europeans were not the ones who took Anatolia, Persia or India in this period.
Trade routes closed and the regions emptied
The regions were not emptied of people; they lost a strong ruler.
Power vacuum.exp: When a strong ruler disappears, rivals rush in. That is a power vacuum.

Rival khanates.q: Which development most weakened Mongol unity from the inside?
Rival khanates.right: Succession fights that divided the empire
wrong: Conversion of every khan to Christianity in the 1300s
The khans adopted local religions such as Islam and Buddhism, not all Christianity.
A single crushing defeat by the young Ottoman army
The Mongols did not fall to one big war; the Ottomans were small at the time.
The invention of gunpowder in western Europe around 1300
Gunpowder came from Song China, and its spread did not split the Mongols.
Rival khanates.exp: The Mongols fell apart rather than losing one war. Family fights split the empire into four khanates.

Mongol assimilation.q: The Il-khans became Muslim and the Yuan rulers adopted Chinese court customs. How did this affect Mongol power?
wrong: It made the khanates reunite under one khan
Adopting different local customs pulled the khanates further apart.
It ended all trade on the Silk Roads
Trade weakened for other reasons, such as plague; customs did not end it.
It let them conquer western Europe
The Mongols never conquered western Europe.
Mongol assimilation.exp: Blending into the local cultures meant the Mongols no longer acted as one people.

Ming expulsion of the Mongols (1368).q: Which event ended Mongol rule in China?
wrong: The Manchu conquest of 1644
The Manchus overthrew the Ming, not the Mongols.
The fall of Constantinople in 1453
That was the end of the Byzantine Empire, far from China.
Timur's raids into India
Timur raided Persia and India; he did not end Mongol rule in China.
Ming expulsion of the Mongols (1368).exp: Rebels drove the Mongols out in 1368 and founded the Ming.

Timur (Tamerlane).q: Which later empire was founded by a descendant of the conqueror who crushed the Ottomans in 1402?
wrong: The Safavid Empire
The Safavids were founded by Ismail I, not by a descendant of Timur.
The Qing Empire
The Qing were founded by the Manchus of northeast China.
The Songhai Empire
Songhai was a West African state with no link to Timur.
Timur (Tamerlane).exp: Babur, founder of the Mughals, descended from Timur and from Genghis Khan.

Ghazi ideal.q: Historians say the founders of the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal states followed a model of the warrior for the faith. What does this model help explain?
Ghazi ideal.right: Why their expansion had a religious purpose
wrong: Why their rulers rejected Islam in favor of steppe gods
The model is a fighter for Islam, so it supports Islam.
Why they relied on navies more than on land armies
The model comes from the land-based steppes, not the sea.
Why they avoided war with their Muslim and Christian neighbors
The model glorifies fighting, not avoiding it.
Ghazi ideal.exp: The ghazi ideal joined steppe warfare to holy war for Islam.

Gunpowder's origin.q: Why did Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal armies all have access to cannons by the 1500s?
Gunpowder's origin.right: Gunpowder spread west along Mongol networks
wrong: All three empires invented gunpowder separately at about the same time
Gunpowder came from one place, Song China.
The Portuguese sold it to all three in the early 1400s
It spread overland through Mongol networks long before most Portuguese contact.
Byzantine engineers taught it to their Turkish neighbors
The Byzantines were the targets of Ottoman cannons, not the source.
Gunpowder's origin.exp: This connects Unit 1 (Song inventions) and Unit 2 (Mongol networks) to Unit 3.

Shared roots of the Islamic empires.q: Which statement best describes a similarity among the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal founders?
Shared roots of the Islamic empires.right: They came from Turkic nomadic roots
wrong: They all followed Shi'a Islam as the state faith
Only the Safavids were Shi'a; the Ottomans and Mughals were Sunni.
They all ruled Hindu majorities in South Asia
Only the Mughals ruled a Hindu majority.
They all built large navies to control the Indian Ocean
The Safavids had no real navy.
Shared roots of the Islamic empires.exp: All three descended from Turkic nomads, used gunpowder, and filled spaces left by the Mongols.

Osman.q: The name of the empire that took Constantinople comes from which founder?
wrong: Mehmed II, the sultan who took the city in 1453
Mehmed II conquered Constantinople, but the empire already had its name.
Selim I, the victor at Chaldiran in 1514
Selim I won at Chaldiran; he did not found the state.
Ismail I, the young ruler crowned in 1501
Ismail I founded the Safavid Empire.
Osman.exp: Osman's small border state became the Ottoman Empire.

Armed trade.q: Two empires exchange goods, but each keeps warships nearby in case the other blocks its merchants. What is this practice called?
wrong: Free trade
Free markets came later and did not rely on threats of force.
Tax farming
Tax farming is a way of collecting taxes, not of trading.
A tribute system
Tribute is payment from a weaker state, not trade backed by force.
Armed trade.exp: Armed trade mixes commerce with readiness to fight, unlike later free markets.

Gunpowder empires.q: Your study guide names three of these states; your textbook adds Russia. What do all of them share?
wrong: All were ruled by Muslim dynasties
Russia was Orthodox Christian.
All were sea-based empires that relied on navies
They were land-based empires; sea empires are Unit 4.
All were made up of a single ethnic group
They ruled many ethnic and religious groups.
Gunpowder empires.exp: The label comes from how they expanded: cannons and muskets.

Mehmed II.q: Which ruler used a 26-foot bronze cannon to break walls that had stood for centuries?
wrong: Suleiman I
Suleiman ruled later (1520–1566) and besieged Vienna.
Shah Abbas I
Abbas was a Safavid shah in Persia.
Babur
Babur used cannons at Panipat in India, not against city walls.
Mehmed II.exp: Mehmed II's cannons broke Constantinople's triple walls in 1453.

Fall of Constantinople (1453).q: Why did the Ottoman capture of this city matter for trade?
Fall of Constantinople (1453).right: It controlled the Black Sea passage
wrong: It opened the first route to the Americas
Routes to the Americas were opened by Europeans at sea.
It gave the Ottomans Mecca and Medina
The holy cities came later, from the Mamluks in 1516–1517.
It ended trade on the Silk Roads
Istanbul remained the western end of the Silk Roads.
Fall of Constantinople (1453).exp: Istanbul controlled the Bosporus, the only waterway linking the Aegean and Black Seas.

Hagia Sophia.q: Mehmed II turned the city's greatest church into a mosque. What does this act most clearly show?
Hagia Sophia.right: A change in who held power
wrong: Continuity of Byzantine religion
Converting it marked a break, not a continuity.
A failed Ottoman siege
The siege of 1453 succeeded.
Ottoman rejection of architecture
The Ottomans kept and restored the building.
Hagia Sophia.exp: The conversion signaled that a new, Muslim dynasty now ruled the city.

Selim I.q: Which conquest gave the Ottomans a strong claim to lead Sunni Islam?
wrong: Taking Constantinople from the Byzantines in 1453
That gave a capital and trade, not the holy cities.
Winning the Battle of Mohács against Hungary in 1526
Mohács gave them Hungary, a Christian land.
Besieging the Habsburg capital of Vienna in 1529
The Vienna siege failed and had no link to the holy cities.
Selim I.exp: Control of Mecca and Medina came with the Mamluk lands.

Suleiman the Magnificent.q: Under which ruler did the Ottomans reach their greatest power and push deepest into Europe?
wrong: Mehmed II, the Conqueror
Mehmed took Constantinople but did not reach Hungary or Vienna.
Osman, the founder
Osman founded a small border state around 1300.
Selim I, conqueror of the Mamluks
Selim pushed east and south, against the Safavids and Mamluks.
Suleiman the Magnificent.exp: Suleiman's reign (1520–1566) was the Ottoman peak.

Battle of Mohács (1526).q: Which victory brought the Ottomans to the edge of Austria?
wrong: Chaldiran, 1514
Chaldiran was fought in Persia against the Safavids.
Lepanto, 1571
Lepanto was an Ottoman naval defeat.
Panipat, 1526
Panipat was Babur's victory in India, the same year.
Battle of Mohács (1526).exp: Winning Hungary at Mohács set up the siege of Vienna three years later.

Siege of Vienna (1529).q: Which event marks the farthest Ottoman advance into Central Europe under Suleiman?
Siege of Vienna (1529).right: The failed siege of Vienna in 1529
wrong: The capture of the island of Rhodes in 1522
Rhodes is an island in the eastern Mediterranean.
The fall of the Byzantine capital in 1453
That was in southeastern Europe, not Central Europe.
The victory over the Hungarians at Mohács in 1526
Mohács came before Vienna and was not the farthest point.
Siege of Vienna (1529).exp: Vienna (1529) failed; the Ottomans never took it.

Ismail I.q: A new ruler in Persia makes Shi'a Islam the official faith in 1501. Which neighbor is most likely to see this as a threat?
wrong: The Hindu Maratha kingdoms
The Marathas were in India and fought the Mughals.
The Russian tsars
Russia was Orthodox Christian and far to the north.
The Manchu banners
The Manchus were in northeast Asia.
Ismail I.exp: Ismail I's Shi'a state set up the Sunni–Shi'a rivalry with the Ottomans.

Shah Abbas I.q: After the Safavids lost at Chaldiran, which ruler modernized their army with gunpowder weapons?
wrong: Ismail I, the founder
Ismail lost at Chaldiran; the army was rebuilt later.
Selim I, the Ottoman victor
Selim was the Ottoman sultan who won at Chaldiran.
Akbar, the Mughal emperor
Akbar was a Mughal emperor in India.
Shah Abbas I.exp: Abbas learned from Chaldiran and added cannons, muskets and ghulams.

Isfahan.q: Abbas I moved his capital in 1598 and filled it with grand buildings. Which city?
wrong: Istanbul
Istanbul was the Ottoman capital.
Delhi
Delhi was a Mughal capital.
Tabriz
Tabriz became a border city between Sunni and Shi'a lands.
Isfahan.exp: Abbas moved the capital from Qazvin to Isfahan.

Shah.q: A source calls the ruler of Persia by a Persian royal title. Which title?
wrong: Sultan
Sultan is a Muslim ruler's title used by the Ottomans.
Tsar
Tsar is the Russian title.
Shogun
Shogun is the Japanese military ruler.
Shah.exp: Safavid rulers were shahs; Ottoman rulers were sultans.

Safavid weaknesses.q: Which feature most separated the Safavids from the Ottomans as a military power?
Safavid weaknesses.right: The Safavids had no real navy
wrong: The Safavids never used firearms
Abbas I armed the Safavids with muskets and artillery.
The Safavids had no capital city
Isfahan was their capital.
The Safavids ruled no Muslims
The Safavids were a Shi'a Muslim state.
Safavid weaknesses.exp: The Ottomans had a strong navy; the Safavids had almost none.

Babur.q: Why is the Mughal founder's ancestry useful for a contextualization sentence?
Babur.right: It links Mughal rule to the Mongols
wrong: It shows the Mughals were Hindu
The Mughal rulers were Muslim.
It proves the Mughals were Persian Shi'a
The Mughals were Sunni.
It connects the Mughals to the Ming
The Ming were Chinese and unrelated.
Babur.exp: Babur descended from Timur and Genghis Khan; 'Mughal' comes from 'Mongol.'

First Battle of Panipat (1526).q: Which battle shows that gunpowder let a small army found a new empire?
wrong: Chaldiran, 1514
Chaldiran was a battle between two existing empires.
Tondibi, 1591
Tondibi ended an empire rather than founding one.
Lepanto, 1571
Lepanto was a sea battle the Ottomans lost.
First Battle of Panipat (1526).exp: At Panipat Babur beat Ibrahim Lodi with cannons and matchlocks.

Akbar.q: A Muslim ruler of a Hindu-majority land ends the tax on non-Muslims and gives Hindus government posts. What was his main goal?
wrong: Converting all Hindus to Islam
He ended a tax that pressured Hindus; he did not force conversion.
Weakening his own army
His tolerance won Hindu nobles to his side.
Preparing to invade Persia
His policy targeted his own subjects, not Persia.
Akbar.exp: Akbar's tolerance won Hindu loyalty in a diverse empire.

Aurangzeb.q: Which ruler made the Mughal Empire its largest yet left it weaker?
wrong: Akbar
Akbar expanded the empire and stabilized it through tolerance.
Shah Jahan
Shah Jahan is best known for building the Taj Mahal.
Babur
Babur founded the empire in 1526.
Aurangzeb.exp: Aurangzeb's wars in the south drained the treasury and his intolerance sparked revolts.

Origin of the name Mughal.q: Which word is the root of the name of the Muslim dynasty that ruled India from 1526?
wrong: Mamluk
The Mamluks ruled Egypt and Syria.
Manchu
The Manchus founded the Qing in China.
Maratha
The Marathas were Hindu rivals of the dynasty.
Origin of the name Mughal.exp: The name points back to Babur's Mongol ancestors.

Banner system.q: Which institution organized the army that took Beijing in 1644?
wrong: The Janissary corps
Janissaries were Ottoman soldiers.
The Cossack bands
Cossacks fought for Russia in Siberia.
The ghulam regiments
Ghulams served the Safavid shahs.
Banner system.exp: Nurhaci's banners were both army units and administrative units.

Manchu conquest of China (1644).q: Why did the Qing rulers have to work hard to prove their right to rule?
Manchu conquest of China (1644).right: They were a minority from outside China
wrong: They had no army to defend Beijing
Their banner armies took and held Beijing.
They had rejected the civil service exam
The Qing kept the exam.
They had lost the Mandate of Heaven to the Ming
The Qing replaced the Ming and claimed the Mandate.
Manchu conquest of China (1644).exp: As foreign rulers of a Han majority, the Manchus needed legitimacy.

Kangxi.q: Which ruler presided over a long period of Qing stability and expansion that included Taiwan and Tibet?
wrong: Qianlong
Qianlong ruled later (1736–1796) and annexed Xinjiang.
Hongwu
Hongwu founded the Ming dynasty in 1368.
Kublai Khan
Kublai founded the Yuan dynasty.
Kangxi.exp: Kangxi took Taiwan in 1683 and extended control into Tibet.

Qianlong.q: Which development weakened the Qing treasury late in the 1700s?
Qianlong.right: Failed campaigns in Burma and Vietnam
wrong: The loss of Taiwan to a Japanese invasion
The Qing held Taiwan in this period.
The decision to end the civil service exam
The exam continued until 1905.
Large tribute payments sent to the Mughal court
The Qing received tribute; they did not pay the Mughals.
Qianlong.exp: Qianlong's costly southern campaigns drained the treasury.

Zunghars.q: Which group was the Qing's main rival on the Central Asian steppe?
wrong: The Hindu Marathas of the Deccan
The Marathas fought the Mughals in India.
The Pashtun rebels of Afghanistan
Pashtun rebels sacked the Safavid capital.
The Mamluk sultans of Egypt and Syria
The Mamluks were conquered by the Ottomans.

Ivan IV.q: Which ruler first pushed Russia east by taking khanates ruled by descendants of the Golden Horde?
wrong: Peter the Great
Peter ruled later (1682–1725) and looked west.
Kangxi
Kangxi was a Qing emperor.
Suleiman I
Suleiman was an Ottoman sultan.
Ivan IV.exp: Ivan IV took Kazan and Astrakhan in the 1550s.

Cossacks.q: Which group fought local peoples and the Siberian khan so Russia could control the fur trade?
wrong: Janissaries
Janissaries were Ottoman soldiers.
Boyars
Boyars were Russian nobles, not frontier fighters.
Samurai
Samurai were Japanese warriors.
Cossacks.exp: The Stroganovs hired Cossacks to fight in Siberia.

Russian push to the Pacific.q: What mainly drove Russian expansion across Siberia?
wrong: The search for a Shi'a holy city
Russia was Orthodox Christian.
Gold from West Africa
West African gold drew Morocco, not Russia.
Silver from Potosí
Potosí silver is in South America.
Russian push to the Pacific.exp: Ivan IV wanted to control the fur trade, and traders kept pushing east.

Control of the Volga.q: How did gaining the river that flows into the Caspian Sea help Russia?
Control of the Volga.right: It allowed direct trade with Persia
wrong: It gave Russia a warm-water Baltic port
St. Petersburg on the Baltic came later under Peter.
It ended Russian serfdom
Serfdom grew worse in this period.
It linked Russia to the Pacific
The Volga flows south into the Caspian, not east.
Control of the Volga.exp: The Volga let Moscow trade south without the Crimean Tatars in the way.

Songhai.q: Why did Timbuktu flourish under this West African empire?
Songhai.right: Rulers backed trade and Islamic scholarship
wrong: It was the Ottoman capital in North Africa
Timbuktu was never an Ottoman capital.
It was the center of the global silver trade
The trade was in gold and salt.
It was protected by a large Songhai navy on the coast
Songhai was a land empire on the Niger River.
Songhai.exp: Songhai rulers supported trade and learning, so Timbuktu became a center of both.

Battle of Tondibi (1591).q: Which battle shows that gunpowder decided wars outside Eurasia too?
wrong: Chaldiran, 1514
Chaldiran was in Persia, in Eurasia.
Panipat, 1526
Panipat was in northern India, in Eurasia.
Mohács, 1526
Mohács was in Hungary, in Europe.
Battle of Tondibi (1591).exp: Morocco's arquebuses defeated Songhai in West Africa.

Moroccan invasion of Songhai.q: What was Morocco's main goal when it invaded the Songhai Empire?
Moroccan invasion of Songhai.right: Control of the gold trade routes
wrong: Spreading Shi'a Islam across the Sahara
Both states were Sunni Muslim.
Gaining a port on the Pacific Ocean
West Africa does not border the Pacific.
Stopping Portuguese missionaries in Timbuktu and Gao
The invasion was about trade, not missionaries.

Battle of Chaldiran (1514).q: After losing this battle, the Safavids rebuilt their army with muskets and cannons. What does this show?
Battle of Chaldiran (1514).right: Defeat pushed rivals to adopt gunpowder
wrong: Cavalry was more effective than gunpowder weapons
The cavalry lost; that is why the Safavids changed.
The Ottomans gave up firearms after their victory
The Ottomans kept their artillery.
Religion played no part at all in the war between them
The battle was also a Sunni versus Shi'a clash.
Battle of Chaldiran (1514).exp: Losing to guns at Chaldiran made the Safavids adopt guns.

Ottoman–Safavid rivalry.q: Which statement best explains the long conflict between the Ottomans and the Safavids?
wrong: It was only a dispute about religious doctrine
Your textbook says it was also about territory and trade routes.
It was only a contest over the West African gold trade
The gold trade is a West African issue.
It was mainly about which of them would control India
India was ruled by the Mughals.
Ottoman–Safavid rivalry.exp: Each side saw the other's Islam as heresy, and they also fought over land and trade.

Trade embargo.q: The Ottomans banned trade with Safavid silk merchants. What does this show about the rivalry?
Trade embargo.right: It was economic as well as religious
wrong: The two empires had no contact at all
An embargo only matters because trade existed.
The Safavids controlled the Bosporus
The Ottomans held the Bosporus.
Silk was banned by Islamic law
The ban targeted a rival, not silk itself.
Trade embargo.exp: Economic pressure was part of the rivalry.

Tabriz (1541).q: Your textbook says a city in Persia became part of the line between Sunni and Shi'a societies. Which city?
wrong: Isfahan
Isfahan was the Safavid capital, deep inside Persia.
Kandahar
Kandahar was fought over by the Safavids and Mughals.
Istanbul
Istanbul was the Ottoman capital.
Tabriz (1541).exp: The Ottomans stopped the Safavids at Tabriz in 1541.

Kandahar.q: Which place was at the center of the Safavid–Mughal rivalry?
wrong: Constantinople, on the Bosporus
That city was taken by the Ottomans.
Vienna, in Austria
Vienna was an Ottoman target.
Timbuktu, on the Niger
Timbuktu was a Songhai city.

Humayun.q: The Safavid shah sheltered the exiled Mughal ruler and helped him regain his throne. What does this show?
wrong: The two empires shared one ruler
They had separate rulers.
The Mughals were Shi'a like the Safavids
The Mughals were Sunni.
Religion caused all their conflicts
Their cooperation shows the relationship was more complicated.
Humayun.exp: Rivalry was not constant; the Safavids helped Humayun in 1555.

Mughal–Maratha conflict.q: How did the Marathas contribute to Mughal decline?
wrong: They converted the emperors to Hinduism
The Mughal emperors stayed Muslim.
They captured Kandahar
Kandahar was taken by the Safavids.
They brought British rule in 1526
1526 is when Babur founded the empire.
Mughal–Maratha conflict.exp: Guerrilla war in the Deccan was costly and helped weaken the empire.

Battle of Lepanto (1571).q: Which event showed that European sea power could defeat the Ottomans?
wrong: Mohács, 1526
Mohács was an Ottoman land victory.
Chaldiran, 1514
Chaldiran was an Ottoman victory over the Safavids.
The capture of Rhodes, 1522
The Ottomans won Rhodes.
Battle of Lepanto (1571).exp: Lepanto was an Ottoman naval defeat after Suleiman's death.

Second siege of Vienna (1683).q: Your textbook says the Ottomans failed to take Vienna twice. What did the second failure mark?
Second siege of Vienna (1683).right: The start of Ottoman retreat in Europe
wrong: The Ottomans' farthest push ever into Central Europe
The 1529 siege was already their farthest push.
The founding of the first Ottoman navy in the Mediterranean
The navy existed long before.
The fall of the Safavid capital to Afghan rebels
Isfahan fell in 1722 to Afghan rebels.
Second siege of Vienna (1683).exp: 1529 was the high-water mark; 1683 was the turning point.

Harem politics.q: Which problem made Ottoman successions weaker after Suleiman?
Harem politics.right: Rival mothers pushing their own sons
wrong: A law banning sultans from having sons
No such law existed.
The end of the devshirme in 1453
The devshirme expanded in the 1400s and 1500s.
Elections of sultans by Janissaries
Sultans were not elected.
Harem politics.exp: Harem politics made some women powerful behind the scenes and weakened succession.

Sick Man of Europe.q: A cartoonist calls an empire that once besieged Vienna weak and dying. Which empire?
wrong: The Russian Empire under the Romanovs
Russia modernized and stayed strong.
The Qing Empire of the Manchus
The nickname refers to an empire in Europe.
The Safavid Empire of Persia
The Safavids never besieged Vienna.
Sick Man of Europe.exp: The nickname described the Ottomans' decline.

Fall of Isfahan (1722).q: Which event shows the Safavid Empire's collapse after Abbas I?
Fall of Isfahan (1722).right: Pashtun rebels sacking the capital in 1722
wrong: Morocco invading Persia across the Sahara in 1591
Morocco invaded Songhai.
The Mughals capturing Istanbul from the Ottomans
The Mughals never took Istanbul.
Ismail I founding the empire as a teenager in 1501
That was its beginning, in 1501.
Fall of Isfahan (1722).exp: Weak shahs and falling revenue led to the 1722 sack of Isfahan.

Why Russia survived.q: Your textbook explains why Russia outlasted the three Islamic gunpowder empires. Which reason does it give?
Why Russia survived.right: Russia rebuilt its army on Western models
wrong: Russia avoided using gunpowder weapons entirely
Russia relied on firearms too.
Russia had the largest and strongest navy in all of Asia
The textbook's reason is army reform.
Russia converted to Islam to win over its southern neighbors
Russia remained Orthodox Christian.
Why Russia survived.exp: Military modernization let Russia survive as an independent state.

Devshirme.q: Why were officials recruited this way loyal to the sultan alone?
Devshirme.right: They had no ties to noble families
wrong: They were elected by local towns
They were taken by force, not elected.
They were the sultan's own relatives
They came from Christian peasant families.
They owned large private estates
Their position depended on the sultan, not on land.
Devshirme.exp: Cut off from their families, they owed everything to the sultan.

Janissaries.q: Which force was key to Ottoman victories at Constantinople and Chaldiran?
wrong: The Qizilbash of Persia
The Qizilbash were Safavid warriors.
The oprichnina of Ivan IV
The oprichnina served Ivan IV in Russia.
The banners of the Manchus
The banners were Manchu units.
Janissaries.exp: Janissaries were gunpowder infantry loyal to the sultan.

Ghulams.q: Which institution is the closest Safavid parallel to the Janissaries?
wrong: The zamindars
Zamindars were Mughal tax collectors.
The daimyo
Daimyo were Japanese lords.
The boyars
Boyars were Russian nobles.
Ghulams.exp: Both were elites recruited from minorities and tied directly to the ruler.

Qizilbash.q: Why did Shah Abbas build a slave army instead of relying only on the warriors who founded the empire?
Qizilbash.right: The founders were loyal to their clans
wrong: The founders refused to fight on horseback
The point is loyalty, not horses.
The founding warriors were Christian converts
The Qizilbash were Muslim.
The founding warriors lived far away in India
They were in Persia.
Qizilbash.exp: Slave soldiers offset troops loyal to tribes or local leaders.

Men of the pen.q: Where did the Safavid shahs find their civilian officials?
wrong: Among Christian boys from the Balkans
That was the Ottoman devshirme.
Through a Confucian exam
That was the Chinese system.
From the samurai class
Samurai were Japanese.
Men of the pen.exp: The Safavids drew on educated Persians for their bureaucracy.

Civil service exam (Qing).q: Why did the Manchu rulers keep China's traditional test for officials?
Civil service exam (Qing).right: To look legitimate to Han Chinese
wrong: To give Manchus every top government job
The exam was open to Han scholars.
Because the Yuan dynasty had relied on it heavily
The Yuan sidelined the exam.
To train Janissaries for the imperial army
Janissaries were Ottoman.
Civil service exam (Qing).exp: Keeping the exam made the Qing look like proper Chinese rulers.

Manchu–Han shared posts.q: How did the Qing reduce resistance from their Han Chinese majority?
Manchu–Han shared posts.right: By sharing offices with Han officials
wrong: By banning Han Chinese from the government
The Qing included Han officials.
By ending Confucian rituals at the imperial court
The Qing adopted Confucian rituals.
By moving the capital from Beijing back to Manchuria
The capital stayed in Beijing.
Manchu–Han shared posts.exp: Sharing posts was a legitimacy strategy.

Oprichnina.q: Ivan IV recruited a loyal force from outside the noble class. Which Ottoman system had a similar goal?
wrong: Tax farming
Tax farming raised money; it was not a loyal force.
The millet system
Millets let religious groups govern themselves.
The jizya
The jizya was a tax on non-Muslims.
Oprichnina.exp: Both created servants loyal only to the ruler, not to nobles.

Boyars.q: Ivan IV forced opponents to move to Moscow and Peter the Great required them to serve in his government. Which group?
wrong: The Cossacks
Cossacks were frontier warriors.
The serfs
Serfs were peasants bound to the land.
The Streltsy
The Streltsy were a military corps.
Boyars.exp: Russian rulers kept the boyars close to control them, like Louis XIV at Versailles.

Table of Ranks.q: Which reform weakened the hold of birth on Russian government jobs?
wrong: Ivan IV's black-clad oprichnina
The oprichnina was a loyal force, not a promotion system.
The new head tax on peasants in 1718
The head tax raised money from peasants.
Peter's creation of the Holy Synod for the Church
The Synod controlled the Church.

Intendants.q: Which officials let French kings control the provinces directly?
wrong: Justices of the peace
Those were English officials chosen from the gentry.
Zamindars
Zamindars served the Mughals.
Daimyo
Daimyo were Japanese lords.
Intendants.exp: Richelieu and Louis XIII expanded the intendant system.

Justices of the peace.q: How did Tudor monarchs govern the English counties?
Justices of the peace.right: Through gentry officials who enforced royal law
wrong: Through Janissaries sent out from the royal court
Janissaries were Ottoman.
Through officials chosen by a Confucian exam
That was China.
Through tax farmers who bid for each English county
